sql:
SELECT z.LocationID, z.Borough, z.Zone, COUNT(t.PULocationID) AS cash_trips
FROM ops.zones z
LEFT JOIN lake.trips t ON t.PULocationID = z.LocationID AND t.payment_type = 2
GROUP BY z.LocationID, z.Borough, z.Zone
ORDER BY z.LocationID

SELECT z.LocationID, z.Borough, z.Zone, COALESCE(agg.cnt, 0) AS cash_trips
FROM ops.zones z
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT PULocationID, COUNT(*) AS cnt
    FROM lake.trips
    WHERE payment_type = 2
    GROUP BY PULocationID
) agg ON agg.PULocationID = z.LocationID
ORDER BY z.LocationID

diagnosis.bottleneck: The query spends most of its time scanning the trips table (495k rows) to filter payment_type=2, then hash-joining the 99k matching rows to the tiny zones table (265 rows) and grouping. The sequential scan on trips is the largest data movement.

plan_nodes.note: Join Type: RIGHT | Conditions: CAST(PULocationID AS BIGINT) = LocationID | Estimated Cardinality: 99167

hypotheses.claim: A filter on the joined side sits in the ON clause of a LEFT JOIN; the join dominates the cost. (matched: left join lake.trips t on … and t.payment_type = 2)

The sequential scan on trips reads all rows to evaluate payment_type=2; creating an index on payment_type (if DuckDB supported secondary indexes) or partitioning the table by payment_type would avoid the full scan.
The join condition CAST(PULocationID AS BIGINT) = LocationID forces a per-row cast on the 99k probe rows; aligning the data types of PULocationID and LocationID would eliminate this CPU overhead.
The hash group by processes 99k rows with string columns (Borough, Zone) in the grouping key; replacing those with integer surrogates (e.g., zone_id) would reduce hash/comparison cost.
